summary: On 26 August 2026 ice and rock fell from Langtang Lirung and dammed the Lende Khola on the Nepal-China border. The water burst through and ran about 100 km down the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli as a wall of mud and boulders. This is the hardest kind of disaster for a radar satellite to see, and the story shows why.

points.title: The path of the mud
points.headline: 100 km, from a mountain to the plains
points.what_happened: The dashed line is the route the debris flow took through this window: down the Lende Khola to the border, then south along the Bhote Koshi past Timure and Syabrubesi. Reported deaths range from about 400 in early counts to more than 1,000, with thousands missing.

sources.label: USGS: 2026 Nepal debris avalanche and flash flood

points.title: Rasuwagadhi: the border crossing
points.headline: Buried on the ground. Invisible from orbit.
points.what_happened: The Lende Khola meets the Bhote Koshi here, at the crossing between Nepal and China. The flow tore through it: buildings, the port area and the highway linking the two countries were buried or destroyed.

sources.label: USGS: 2026 Nepal debris avalanche and flash flood

points.title: Why the radar missed it
points.headline: A river of mud narrower than one pixel
points.what_happened: At Timure the valley floor is a few tens of metres wide between walls more than a kilometre high. Each radar pixel here is 20 m, so the mud fills one or two pixels at most, and the steep walls throw radar shadow over the valley floor. Radar is strong on wide changes, such as floods and burns; a thin line at the bottom of a gorge is its blind spot. An honest map has to say so.

sources.label: Maps of Nepal: anatomy of the disaster

points.title: Syabrubesi: where the valley opens
points.headline: Here the radar does see change
points.what_happened: The trailhead town for the Langtang trek, where the valley is wider. Downstream of here 11 hydropower stations and one solar plant, 431 MW in all, stopped operating, and UNDP estimated at least 2.2 million tonnes of debris.

points.title: So why use radar at all?
points.headline: It was the monsoon: cameras saw cloud
points.what_happened: These are ordinary satellite photos of the two dates. Drag the handle. Where the sky was clear a camera shows the scar better than radar does, but in the monsoon clear days are rare, and a disaster does not wait for one. That is why this map uses radar and not only photos: a camera needs daylight and a clear sky, while radar sends its own signal, which passes through cloud, smoke and darkness and comes back the same in any weather. The source of this flow, the collapse on Langtang Lirung, shows clearly in the radar: open that event next.
